title: RTOS & Real-Time Concepts
relevance: Tests whether a candidate understands deadline-driven correctness, preemptive scheduling, and concurrency hazards that show up in embedded and systems SDE interviews.

phases.goal: Establish what makes a system real-time and when a bare-metal superloop is insufficient.

must_hit.point: A real-time system requires both logical correctness and meeting a strict deadline; determinism matters more than raw throughput.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts a fast non-deadline computation with a controller that fails if it misses its timing budget.

must_hit.point: Hard real-time treats a missed deadline as total system failure; firm makes the late result useless without destroying the system; soft tolerates degraded performance.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Gives matching examples such as flight control/airbags, dropped late video frames, and UI updates.

must_hit.point: A bare-metal superloop runs handlers sequentially in an infinite main loop, so a slow call can starve later critical work.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes cooperative while(1) sequencing and how one long handler delays the next.

must_hit.point: An RTOS adds preemptive multitasking so a high-priority task can interrupt a low-priority one and bound response time when independent timing events get too complex for a linear loop.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States you need an RTOS when timing dependencies between independent events outgrow a superloop.

probes: What distinguishes a real-time system from a system that is merely fast?
When would you move from a superloop to an RTOS?

hints.1: Think about deadlines, not just throughput.
hints.2: Compare hard, firm, and soft misses, then contrast sequential cooperative looping with preemption.
hints.3: Correctness requires finishing before a deadline; hard/firm/soft differ in consequence of a miss; a superloop starves critical work while an RTOS can preempt.

phases.goal: Explain tasks, scheduling, states, context switches, IPC primitives, and ISR deferral under an RTOS.

must_hit.point: Each RTOS task is an infinite loop with its own private stack and saved CPU-register context so it appears to own the CPU.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions per-task stack plus register context to create concurrent virtual threads on one core.

must_hit.point: A periodic system-tick interrupt (for example every 1ms), or a yield, triggers the scheduler to run the highest-priority ready task.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names the tick and priority-based selection at tick or yield.

must_hit.point: Task states include Running (one per core), Ready, Blocked (waiting for an event), and Suspended (explicitly paused).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Lists all four states with the one-running-per-core rule.

must_hit.point: A context switch pushes the outgoing task's registers onto its stack, saves its stack pointer, loads the incoming stack pointer, and restores its registers—preemptive priority-based scheduling.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Walks through save/restore of registers and stack pointers.

must_hit.point: A blocked delay does not busy-spin; the scheduler marks the task Blocked and gives the CPU to others until the wait ends.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Corrects the while-loop-spin misconception for something like vTaskDelay.

must_hit.point: Mutexes protect shared resources with ownership; semaphores signal without ownership (binary flag or counting resources); queues pass copied data as a thread-safe FIFO; event flags are lightweight bitmasks.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Distinguishes ownership on mutexes, no owner on semaphores, copy-based queues, and bitmask events.

must_hit.point: ISRs preempt everything and must stay short: clear the hardware flag, wake a task via FromISR primitives (semaphore/queue), and never call standard blocking RTOS APIs from an interrupt.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes defer-to-task pattern and FromISR-only calls.

must_hit.point: Interrupt latency is time from hardware trigger to the first ISR instruction; scheduling latency is time from the ISR making a task Ready until that task is Running.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Defines both latencies as the two responsiveness numbers.

probes: Walk through what happens on a context switch when a higher-priority task becomes ready.
How should an ISR interact with RTOS tasks, and what must it never do?

hints.1: Start from per-task stack/context and the scheduler tick.
hints.2: Cover states, then IPC primitives, then why ISR work is deferred via FromISR APIs.
hints.3: Tick/yield picks highest priority; switch saves/restores context; Blocked waits without spinning; ISR clears hardware, gives FromISR, exits; interrupt vs scheduling latency.

phases.goal: Surface priority inversion, deadlock conditions, schedulability limits, and memory allocation choices.

must_hit.point: Priority inversion occurs when a high-priority task waits on a lock held by a low-priority task that is then preempted by a medium-priority task, so the high task effectively runs at the low priority.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Retells VIP/janitor/customer or the Mars Pathfinder 1997 bus mutex story.

must_hit.point: Priority inheritance temporarily elevates the lock-holding low-priority task to the blocked high priority so medium tasks cannot preempt it until the mutex is released.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States elevate-on-block, then drop priority on give.

must_hit.point: Use a mutex rather than a binary semaphore to protect shared resources because only ownership enables priority inheritance and prevents unbounded inversion.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explicitly ties mutex ownership to inheritance support.

must_hit.point: Deadlock needs all four Coffman conditions: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption of locks, and circular wait; consistent lock ordering breaks circular wait.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Lists the four conditions and the acquire-order fix.

must_hit.point: Under rate-monotonic scheduling, shorter-period tasks get higher priority; if utilization stays below roughly 69%, independent tasks are mathematically guaranteed to meet deadlines.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States shortest-period-highest-priority and the roughly 69% bound.

must_hit.point: Dynamic malloc/free is discouraged because it is non-deterministic and risks heap fragmentation; high-reliability systems statically allocate stacks and queues at compile time.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Rejects heap allocation for timing predictability and fragmentation risk.

probes: Explain priority inversion and how priority inheritance fixes it.
Why is a mutex preferred over a binary semaphore for protecting a shared resource?

hints.1: Picture high blocked on low while medium runs.
hints.2: Connect inversion to inheritance/ceiling and mutex ownership; mention Coffman or RMS if you go deeper.
hints.3: Medium preempts the lock holder → unbounded wait; inheritance boosts the holder; mutex ownership enables that; order locks to break circular wait; RMS uses short period → high priority with roughly 69% utilization bound.

phases.goal: Apply RTOS patterns to concrete task communication, inheritance timelines, and deferred interrupt handling.

must_hit.point: Producer/consumer tasks should exchange data through a queue: sender may block briefly if full, receiver can block until data arrives, so the scheduler parks waiting tasks instead of sharing memory unsafely.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes xQueueSend/xQueueReceive-style blocking and copy-based handoff.

must_hit.point: In an inheritance scenario, when High blocks on a mutex held by Low, Low is raised to High's priority so Medium cannot preempt Low until the mutex is given and priorities restore.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Steps through Low takes, High blocks and boosts Low, Medium cannot preempt, give, then High resumes.

must_hit.point: Deferred interrupt processing uses an ISR-safe give (for example xSemaphoreGiveFromISR), optional yield-from-ISR if a higher-priority task woke, and a handler task that takes the semaphore then processes the buffer.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Fills in FromISR give plus portYIELD_FROM_ISR and a blocking handler task.

must_hit.point: Equal highest-priority tasks that never block typically time-slice each tick, wasting CPU on constant context switches.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Warns about round-robin thrashing among always-ready peers.

must_hit.point: Underestimating a task stack risks silent overflow into adjacent task memory such as a Task Control Block; a watchdog timer resets the CPU if software fails to kick it because of deadlock or a hung loop.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Links stack overflow to bizarre crashes and WDT kick/reset as freeze recovery.

probes: Design a safe producer/consumer between two FreeRTOS-style tasks.
How would you structure an ISR and handler task for DMA completion?

hints.1: Prefer queues or FromISR signaling over shared buffers in the ISR.
hints.2: Sketch block-on-queue/semaphore paths and what inheritance does while a mutex is held.
hints.3: Queue send/receive with blocking; inheritance boosts Low until give; ISR uses GiveFromISR and yield-from-ISR; handler takes then processes; watch equal-priority thrash, stack overflow, and watchdog kick.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: A superloop is simple cooperative sequencing but one slow handler delays everything; an RTOS preempts by priority so independent deadline-driven events stay responsive when the linear loop becomes too complex.

tradeoffs.topic: Mutex vs binary semaphore for shared resources
tradeoffs.strong_answer: A binary semaphore has no owner, so the RTOS cannot apply priority inheritance; a mutex has ownership and can elevate the holder, preventing unbounded priority inversion.
malloc/free take variable time and can fragment the heap, breaking determinism; statically allocating stacks and queues at compile time keeps timing predictable in high-reliability systems.

tradeoffs.topic: Process work in ISR vs defer to a task
tradeoffs.strong_answer: ISRs preempt everything and must stay short—clear the flag and wake a task via FromISR APIs; heavy processing belongs in a high-priority handler task so interrupt and scheduling latency stay bounded.
Overestimating wastes scarce SRAM; underestimating causes stack overflow that can silently corrupt an adjacent task's memory (often the TCB) and produce hard-to-debug crashes.

gotchas.trap: Assuming vTaskDelay or other blocked waits spin in a while loop burning CPU.
gotchas.correction: The scheduler marks the task Blocked, swaps it out, and only reschedules it when the wait ends, giving the CPU to other tasks.

gotchas.trap: Two always-ready tasks sharing the exact same highest priority.
gotchas.correction: They typically time-slice every tick and waste cycles on constant context switching.

gotchas.trap: Protecting a shared resource with a binary semaphore and expecting priority inheritance.
gotchas.correction: Without ownership the RTOS cannot inherit priority; use a mutex so the holder can be elevated.

gotchas.trap: Acquiring multiple locks in inconsistent orders across tasks.
gotchas.correction: That enables circular wait; always take locks in the same global order (for example Lock X before Lock Y) to make deadlock impossible.

gotchas.trap: Calling standard blocking RTOS APIs from an ISR.
gotchas.correction: Use only FromISR variants, keep the ISR short, and defer work by giving a semaphore or sending to a queue to a handler task.

gotchas.trap: Relying on malloc/free in hard real-time paths.
gotchas.correction: Allocation time is non-deterministic and fragmentation is a risk; allocate stacks and queues statically at compile time.
